questions.s: Joints of the heads of the ribs (Last's):
o: The lower facet of the head articulates with its own vertebra

The lower facet on the head of a typical rib articulates with the upper border of its own vertebra; the upper facet with the vertebra above.
So rib 6 articulates with T5 and T6.
The intra-articular ligament attaches the ridge to the disc

The intra-articular ligament ties the crest between the two facets of the rib head to the intervertebral disc.
This divides the joint into two cavities.
The first rib articulates with C7 and T1

Last's says the first rib articulates with T1 only, never with C7.
Its head has a single facet.
The radiate ligament of the first rib has three bands

The radiate ligament of the first rib (and of the last two ribs) has two bands, not three, because these ribs articulate with only one vertebra.
Typical ribs have three bands.
It is formed by the central band of the radiate ligament

The central band of the radiate ligament crosses horizontally to meet its fellow of the other side; Last's calls this the hypochordal bow.
It is a morphological remnant.
It runs deep to the anterior longitudinal ligament

The hypochordal bow lies deep to the anterior longitudinal ligament, blending with the disc.
It is not visible from the front.
It explains the formation of the dens

Last's uses the hypochordal bow to explain the anterior arch of the atlas, not the dens.
The anterior arch is an ossified hypochordal bow.
It lies superficial to the anterior longitudinal ligament

The hypochordal bow lies deep to the anterior longitudinal ligament, not superficial to it.
It runs across the disc.
Costochondral joints are primary cartilaginous

Costochondral joints are primary cartilaginous joints; no movement occurs at them.
The rib is continuous with its cartilage.
The first sternocostal joint is primary cartilaginous

The first sternocostal joint is primary cartilaginous, so the manubrium and first ribs move together.
The other sternocostal joints are synovial.
Interchondral synovial joints exist between cartilages 2 to 5

Interchondral synovial joints exist between costal cartilages 6 and 7, 7 and 8, and 8 and 9, not between 2 and 5.
Cartilages 2 to 5 do not touch each other.
The third sternocostal joint has two cavities

It is the second sternocostal joint that has two separate cavities, because it meets the manubriosternal junction.
The third has one cavity.
The upper six are reciprocally curved

The upper six costotransverse joints are reciprocally curved (concave on the transverse process), allowing rotation of the rib neck. Lower down they are flat, allowing gliding.
This explains bucket-handle versus pump-handle movements.
The superior costotransverse ligament runs to the transverse process above

The superior costotransverse ligament runs from the crest of the rib neck to the transverse process above.
It lies in front of the posterior ramus.
The lower two ribs have synovial costotransverse joints

The 11th and 12th ribs have no tubercles and no synovial costotransverse joints, only ligamentous attachments.
They are floating ribs.
The lateral costotransverse ligament attaches to the medial facet of the tubercle

The lateral costotransverse ligament attaches to the lateral, non-articular facet of the rib tubercle, not the medial (articular) facet.
The medial facet forms the synovial joint.
The serratus posterior muscles belong to the outer layer

The serratus posterior muscles belong to the outer layer of the thoracic wall, with the external intercostals.
They are respiratory muscles.
The neurovascular plane lies between middle and inner layers

The intercostal vessels and nerves run between the middle (internal intercostal) and inner (innermost intercostal) layers.
This is the neurovascular plane.
The subcostals belong to the middle layer

The subcostals belong to the inner (transversus thoracis) group, with the innermost intercostals and sternocostalis.
They span more than one space.
The internal intercostals correspond to external oblique

The internal intercostals correspond to internal oblique in the abdominal wall. The external intercostals correspond to external oblique.
The layers are continuous in plan.
The last two costal cartilages are free

Costal cartilages 11 and 12 are free; cartilages 8 to 10 join the cartilage above.
So only seven reach the sternum.
The manubriosternal joint is a symphysis

The manubriosternal joint is a symphysis (secondary cartilaginous joint).
It may ossify in old age.
The upper ten costal cartilages articulate with the sternum

Only the upper seven costal cartilages articulate with the sternum, not ten.
These are the "true" ribs.
Ribs articulate with the vertebral column in one place

Ribs articulate with the vertebral column in two places: at the head (with the bodies) and at the tubercle (with the transverse process).
Except ribs 11 and 12, which have only the head joint.
The inspiratory centre lies near the nucleus of the tractus solitarius

A medullary inspiratory centre near the nucleus of the tractus solitarius sets the rhythm of breathing.
Last's calls it a respiratory "pacemaker".
The pneumotaxic centre lies near the superior cerebellar peduncle

The pontine pneumotaxic centre, near the superior cerebellar peduncle, switches inspiration off to allow expiration.
It fine-tunes the rhythm.
Inspiratory neurons project to the ipsilateral phrenic neurons

Last's says inspiratory neurons project to the contralateral phrenic neurons, not the ipsilateral ones.
The fibres cross in the medulla.
Hypoxia is detected centrally in the medulla

Hypoxia is detected peripherally by the carotid and aortic bodies. The brain responds to carbon dioxide.
Central chemoreceptors sense pH.
Its superficial and deep parts are functionally one

Last's says the superficial and deep cardiac plexuses are only a descriptive division; functionally they are one plexus.
They are continuous.
It includes a pulmonary part supplying bronchial muscle

The cardiac plexus has a pulmonary part that enters the lung root to supply bronchial muscle and the lung vessels.
The pulmonary plexuses are extensions of it.
Its branches reach only the SA node

Cardiac plexus branches reach the SA node, the AV node, the bundle, the ventricles and the coronary arteries, not just the SA node.
Autonomic control reaches all parts of the heart.
Afferent vagal fibres from the lungs have cell bodies in the superior vagal ganglion

Afferent vagal fibres from the lungs have their cell bodies in the inferior vagal ganglion, not the superior one.
The superior ganglion serves only the meningeal and auricular branches.

questions.s: Cutaneous supply of the thoracic wall (Last's):
o: Skin above the second rib is supplied by supraclavicular nerves (C4)

Above the second rib the chest skin is supplied by the supraclavicular nerves (C3, C4). T2 lies just below, across an axial line.
So C4 meets T2 on the front of the chest.
Lateral cutaneous branches emerge in the midaxillary line

The lateral cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves emerge in the midaxillary line, dividing into anterior and posterior branches.
A useful level for blocking them.
The first intercostal nerve has a large lateral cutaneous branch

Last's says the first intercostal nerve has no lateral or anterior cutaneous branch.
Most of T1 goes into the brachial plexus.
The collateral branch supplies skin

The collateral branch of an intercostal nerve has no cutaneous supply; it supplies muscle, pleura and periosteum.
It runs along the upper border of the rib below.
The order from above down is vein, artery, nerve

Under the costal groove the order of the bundle from above down is vein, artery, nerve.
The nerve is lowest.
The collateral branches run along the upper border of the rib below

The collateral branches run along the upper border of the rib below. Chest drains are inserted just above a rib to avoid the main bundle.
The collateral branches are small.
Upper anterior cutaneous branches pass behind the internal thoracic artery

The upper anterior cutaneous branches pass in front of the internal thoracic artery, not behind it.
The artery lies about 1 cm from the sternal edge.
The subcostal lateral cutaneous branch supplies skin over the umbilicus

The lateral cutaneous branch of the subcostal nerve supplies the skin of the anterior buttock between the iliac crest and the greater trochanter, not over the umbilicus.
The umbilicus is T10.
The first two spaces are supplied posteriorly by the superior intercostal artery

The first two intercostal spaces are supplied posteriorly by the superior intercostal artery, from the costocervical trunk.
The aorta supplies the rest.
The musculophrenic artery supplies spaces 7 to 9 anteriorly

The musculophrenic artery supplies the anterior intercostal arteries of spaces 7 to 9; spaces 10 and 11 have none.
The lowest spaces are open in front.
The internal thoracic artery supplies spaces 1 to 9 anteriorly

The internal thoracic artery supplies the anterior intercostal arteries of spaces 1 to 6, not 1 to 9.
The musculophrenic takes over below.
Spaces 10 and 11 have anterior intercostal arteries from the musculophrenic

Spaces 10 and 11 have no anterior intercostal arteries.
Their cartilages do not reach the front.
The first space drains to the supreme intercostal vein

The first intercostal space drains to the supreme (highest) intercostal vein, which joins the brachiocephalic vein.
The next spaces drain to the superior intercostal vein.
The left superior intercostal vein crosses the arch superficial to the vagus

The left superior intercostal vein crosses the aortic arch superficial to the vagus and deep to the phrenic nerve.
It drains to the left brachiocephalic vein.
The right superior intercostal vein drains to the right brachiocephalic vein

The right superior intercostal vein drains into the azygos vein, not the right brachiocephalic vein.
The left one drains into the left brachiocephalic.
Each space has two posterior and one anterior vein

Each intercostal space has one posterior and two anterior intercostal veins, the reverse of the statement.
The anterior veins accompany the paired anterior arteries.

questions.s: At the neck of the first rib, from medial to lateral, lie:
o: The sympathetic trunk (stellate ganglion)

At the neck of the first rib the sympathetic trunk (stellate ganglion) lies most medially.
A Pancoast tumour here can cause Horner's syndrome.
The supreme intercostal vein

Next laterally lies the supreme intercostal vein.
It drains the first space.
The superior intercostal artery

Then comes the superior intercostal artery, from the costocervical trunk.
It supplies the first two spaces.
The internal thoracic artery

The most lateral structure at the neck of the first rib is the T1 anterior ramus, not the internal thoracic artery.
The internal thoracic artery lies far anterior, behind the costal cartilages.
The right crus attaches to L1-3

The larger right crus attaches to the bodies of L1 to L3 and their discs.
It forms the oesophageal opening.
The left crus attaches to L1-2

The left crus attaches to the bodies of L1 and L2.
It is smaller than the right.
The medial arcuate ligament is a thickening of the lumbar fascia

The medial arcuate ligament is a thickening of the psoas fascia. The lateral arcuate ligament is a thickening of the lumbar fascia over quadratus lumborum.
Psoas medial, quadratus lateral.
The median arcuate ligament lies at L2

The median arcuate ligament, joining the two crura in front of the aorta, lies at T12, not L2.
The coeliac trunk arises just below it.
The vena caval opening transmits the right phrenic nerve

The right phrenic nerve passes through the vena caval opening in the central tendon.
It supplies the under surface of the diaphragm.
The oesophageal opening transmits the left gastric vessels

The oesophageal opening transmits the oesophagus, the vagal trunks and the oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels.
A portosystemic anastomosis lies here.
The aortic opening lies at T10

The aortic opening lies at T12, behind the median arcuate ligament, not at T10.
The oesophageal opening is at T10.
The left phrenic nerve passes through the oesophageal opening

The left phrenic nerve pierces the muscle of the left dome of the diaphragm, not the oesophageal opening.
Neither phrenic uses the oesophageal opening.
The phrenic nerves supply it from its abdominal surface

The phrenic nerves pierce the diaphragm and supply it from its abdominal (under) surface.
Their branches run in the muscle below the pleura.
Each half including its crus is supplied by the ipsilateral phrenic

Each half of the diaphragm, including its crus, is supplied by its own phrenic nerve.
So unilateral phrenic palsy paralyses one hemidiaphragm.
The sling of the right crus around the oesophagus is supplied by the right phrenic

The sling of right crus fibres around the oesophagus is supplied by the left phrenic nerve, because those fibres cross from the left.
A Last's detail.
Its morphology is the outer (external oblique) layer

Morphologically the diaphragm belongs to the inner (transversus) layer of the body wall, not the outer (external oblique) layer.
It is continuous in plan with transversus abdominis.
It is plastered to scalenus anterior by prevertebral fascia

The phrenic nerve descends on scalenus anterior beneath the prevertebral fascia, which holds it in place and protects it during neck dissection.
Dissection superficial to the fascia spares it. (Last's p. 442)
About one-third of its fibres are sensory

About a third of phrenic fibres are sensory, from the pericardium, mediastinal and diaphragmatic pleura, and peritoneum.
The rest are motor to the diaphragm. (Last's p. 442)
It passes lateral to the apex of the lung

In the root of the neck the phrenic nerve passes medial to the apex of the lung, in front of the subclavian artery.
The dome of the pleura lies lateral. (Last's p. 442)
It runs behind the lung root

The phrenic nerve runs in front of the lung root. The vagus runs behind it.
"Phrenic in front, vagus behind." (Last's p. 442)

questions.s: Relations of the phrenic nerves in the thorax:
o: The right phrenic lies on venous structures throughout

The right phrenic nerve runs on venous structures throughout: the right brachiocephalic vein, superior vena cava, right atrium and inferior vena cava.
It passes through the caval opening. (Last's p. 442)
The left phrenic lies lateral to the left superior intercostal vein

The left phrenic nerve crosses the aortic arch lateral to (in front of) the left superior intercostal vein and the vagus.
The vein crosses between the two nerves. (Last's p. 442)
The phrenic lies behind the vagus

The phrenic lies anterior to the vagus, not behind it.
On the arch: phrenic in front, vein between, vagus behind. (Last's p. 442)
The left phrenic supplies the visceral serous pericardium

The visceral serous pericardium is insensate; the phrenic supplies the fibrous and parietal serous pericardium only.
Pain arises from the parietal layer. (Last's p. 442)
The right vagus is in contact with the trachea

The right vagus lies directly against the trachea; the left is held away by the great arteries.
The vagi try to reach the midline. (Last's p. 442)
The anterior vagal trunk carries predominantly left vagal fibres

The anterior vagal trunk consists mainly of left vagal fibres and the posterior mainly of right, though both are mixed.
A result of gut rotation. (Last's p. 442)
Both vagi pass in front of the lung roots

Both vagi pass behind the lung roots, not in front.
They help form the posterior pulmonary plexuses. (Last's p. 442)
The right vagus runs superficial to the azygos arch

The right vagus runs deep to the arch of the azygos vein, not superficial to it.
The right phrenic lies superficial. (Last's p. 442)
The superficial plexus lies in front of the ligamentum arteriosum

The superficial cardiac plexus lies in front of the ligamentum arteriosum, below the aortic arch.
It is small. (Last's p. 442)
The deep plexus lies in front of the left main bronchus

The deep cardiac plexus lies in front of the left main bronchus (and tracheal bifurcation), to the right of the ligamentum.
It receives most cardiac nerves. (Last's p. 442)
The superficial plexus receives the right vagal cervical branches

The superficial plexus receives the left inferior cervical vagal branch and the left superior cervical sympathetic branch, not right vagal branches.
All right-sided branches go to the deep plexus. (Last's p. 442)
Cardiac pain afferents travel only with the vagus

Cardiac pain afferents travel with the sympathetic nerves; vagal afferents serve reflexes.
Angina refers to T1 to T5. (Last's p. 442)
It lies on the necks of the ribs

The thoracic sympathetic trunk lies on the necks of the ribs, lateral to their heads.
Lower down it lies on the vertebral bodies. (Last's p. 442)
It lies in front of the intercostal vessels and nerves

It lies in front of the intercostal vessels and nerves.
So the trunk is accessible thoracoscopically for sympathectomy. (Last's p. 442)
It enters the abdomen behind the lateral arcuate ligament

The thoracic sympathetic trunk enters the abdomen behind the medial arcuate ligament, not the lateral.
The subcostal bundle passes behind the lateral one. (Last's p. 442)
It always has 12 ganglia

The thoracic trunk has up to 12 ganglia but often fewer, because of fusion.
The first often fuses with the inferior cervical (stellate). (Last's p. 442)

questions.s: Innervation of the pleura and lungs (Last's):
o: The visceral pleura is insensate

The visceral pleura has only autonomic (vasomotor) supply and is insensitive to pain.
Lung tumours are painless until they reach the parietal pleura. (Last's p. 442)
The mediastinal pleura is supplied by the phrenic

The mediastinal pleura is supplied by the phrenic nerve.
So mediastinal pleurisy may refer pain to the shoulder. (Last's p. 442)
The costal pleura is supplied by the phrenic

The costal pleura is supplied by the intercostal nerves, not the phrenic.
Pain is felt locally on the chest wall. (Last's p. 442)
Sympathetic fibres constrict the bronchi

Sympathetic fibres (T2 to T6) dilate the bronchi; the vagus constricts them.
Beta-agonists relieve bronchospasm. (Last's p. 442)
The jugular notch lies at T3

Last's places the jugular notch at T3 (at the lower border of T2/T3).
It is the upper border of the manubrium. (Last's p. 442)
The sternal angle lies at T4

The sternal angle lies at the level of the T4/5 disc, marking the start and end of the aortic arch and the tracheal bifurcation.
Also the second costal cartilage. (Last's p. 442)
The lower end of the sternum lies at T12

The lower end of the sternum lies at about T8, not T12.
T12 is the level of the aortic opening. (Last's p. 442)
The vena caval opening lies at T12

The vena caval opening lies at T8, not T12.
The aortic opening is at T12. (Last's p. 442)
The lower facet on the head articulates with its own vertebra

The lower facet on the head of a typical rib articulates with its own vertebra; the upper with the vertebra above.
Two demifacets. (Last's p. 442)
The first, eleventh and twelfth ribs have a single facet on the head

Ribs 1, 11 and 12 articulate only with their own vertebrae, so they have a single facet on the head.
Rib 10 often does too. (Last's p. 442)
The 11th and 12th ribs have synovial costotransverse joints

Ribs 11 and 12 have only ligamentous costotransverse attachments and usually no tubercles.
No synovial costotransverse joints. (Last's p. 442)
The tenth rib is always atypical

Last's says the tenth rib is usually typical (it may sometimes have a single facet).
So "always atypical" is wrong. (Last's p. 442)
The lower trunk of the brachial plexus lies in the subclavian groove

The lower trunk of the brachial plexus lies in the subclavian groove of the first rib; the artery touches only its outer border.
A cervical rib or tight scalene can compress the lower trunk. (Last's p. 442)
Scalenus anterior attaches to the scalene tubercle

Scalenus anterior inserts into the scalene tubercle on the inner border of the first rib, between the grooves for the subclavian vein and artery.
It separates vein (front) from artery (behind). (Last's p. 442)
The subclavian artery lies in its groove

The lower trunk of the plexus lies in the groove; the subclavian artery lies a little higher.
Last's makes a point of this. (Last's p. 442)
Scalenus medius attaches in front of the subclavian vein groove

Scalenus medius attaches behind the arterial groove, between it and the tubercle of the rib, not in front of the venous groove.
Scalenus anterior lies between the venous and arterial grooves. (Last's p. 442)
The second rib has a tuberosity for serratus anterior

The second rib has a tuberosity on its outer surface for the first two digitations of serratus anterior.
A useful identifying feature. (Last's p. 442)
The twelfth rib has no angle or costal groove

The short twelfth rib has no angle, tubercle or costal groove.
It may be very short. (Last's p. 442)
The second rib has a tuberosity for scalenus medius

The second rib has a tuberosity for serratus anterior; scalenus posterior attaches to the second rib's upper border, and scalenus medius to the first rib.
So scalenus medius is wrong. (Last's p. 442)
Quadratus lumborum attaches to the lateral part of the twelfth rib

Quadratus lumborum attaches to the medial half of the lower border of the twelfth rib, not the lateral part.
It steadies the rib in inspiration. (Last's p. 442)
Levatores costarum are supplied by posterior rami

Levatores costarum are true back muscles, supplied by posterior rami.
They are the only thoracic wall muscles so supplied. (Last's p. 244-6)
Serratus posterior superior inserts lateral to the angles of ribs 2-5

Serratus posterior superior runs from the C6 to T2 spines to just lateral to the angles of ribs 2 to 5.
It may elevate the ribs. (Last's p. 244-6)
Serratus posterior inferior inserts into ribs 5-8

Serratus posterior inferior inserts into ribs 9 to 12, not 5 to 8.
It runs from the lower thoracic and upper lumbar spines. (Last's p. 244-6)
External intercostals extend forward to the sternum

The external intercostals extend forward only to the costochondral junctions, then are replaced by the anterior intercostal membrane.
They do not reach the sternum. (Last's p. 244-6)
Internal intercostals extend to the side of the sternum

Unlike the externals, the internal intercostals extend forward to the side of the sternum. Behind, they are replaced by the posterior intercostal membrane.
They run down and back. (Last's p. 244-6)
They are replaced posteriorly by the posterior intercostal membrane

Posteriorly, from the angle of the rib to the superior costotransverse ligament, the internal intercostals are replaced by the posterior intercostal membrane.
The bundle is then exposed. (Last's p. 244-6)
Innermost intercostals are wider above than below

The innermost intercostals are wider below than above.
They are poorly developed in the upper spaces. (Last's p. 244-6)
Transversus thoracis arises from the manubrium

Transversus thoracis arises from the lower end of the sternum (and xiphoid), not the manubrium, and fans up to costal cartilages 2 to 6.
It lies behind the internal thoracic vessels. (Last's p. 244-6)
The upper striated muscle is supplied from the nucleus ambiguus

The upper striated muscle of the oesophagus is supplied by nucleus ambiguus fibres in the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves.
It is continuous with the pharynx. (Last's p. 244-6)
The upper part receives sympathetics from the middle cervical ganglion

The upper oesophagus receives sympathetic fibres from the middle cervical ganglion via the inferior thyroid arteries.
The lower part from the thoracic trunk. (Last's p. 244-6)
The lower part receives no sympathetic supply

The lower oesophagus does receive sympathetic supply, from the thoracic trunks and greater splanchnic nerves.
Every part of the gut has sympathetic supply. (Last's p. 244-6)
Sensation travels only via sympathetic fibres

Oesophageal sensation travels via both the vagus (inferior ganglion) and sympathetic fibres.
So vagotomy does not abolish oesophageal pain. (Last's p. 244-6)
